June 28, 2026 | Aqueduct Racetrack, New York, New York

For this caption, I am simply going to copy and paste the caption I used on TikTok. This is not as polished and itâs mostly pure emotion, but I think that is the best approach to anything I could say about Aqueductâs closing day:

âIt honestly did not fully hit me until last night that Aqueduct is closing. So much of the racing history I love most happened there. When I think of Aqueduct, I think of the Sommers. I think of Sigmund and Viola, Pancho Martin, and the horses I have come to hold so dear. Autobiography winning the 1972 Jockey Club Gold Cup. Sham breaking his maiden there in December 1972, then returning for the Wood Memorial the following spring. Rube the Great winning the Wood in 1974. The five Display Handicaps won by Sommer horses. All of those races, winters, and ordinary days between the famous ones feel personal to me. I have spent so much time researching these people and horses, looking for photographs, reading old articles, piecing together races, relationships, and lives. Aqueduct is at the center of so many of those stories. It is where they walked, worked, won, lost, celebrated, and grieved. That is what makes this so difficult. It is not only the loss of a racetrack. It feels like saying goodbye to a physical connection with a world I have spent years trying to understand. Most of the people and horses I associate with Aqueduct are long gone, but standing there still meant standing somewhere they had once stood. I know the future of New York racing is bright, and I am excited to see what comes next at Belmont. But looking forward does not mean leaving something behind is easy. Progress does not erase grief, and a new beginning does not make an ending hurt any less. I am so grateful I was able to be there for Aqueductâs final day, to walk through it and take everything in one last time. Aqueduct gave New York racing more than eight decades of history. It held triumphs, tragedies, champions, longshots, bitter winters, packed grandstands, and quiet mornings. It held the stories that first made me fall so deeply in love with this part of the sport. Goodbye, Aqueduct. Iâll miss you.â

May 2026 | Churchill Downs, Louisville, Kentucky ( @churchilldowns )

Back in May, I finally got to visit Churchill Downs for the first time. Somehow, after all the times Iâve been to Louisville, I had never actually made it to the track before.

We drove about 11 hours to Kentucky (for something entirely unrelated, we were there for an archery tournament) and then went almost immediately for Twilight Thursday, which honestly ended up being the perfect way to experience Churchill for the first time, at least in my opinion. Getting there in the evening, watching the horses come through the paddock, hearing the races, and seeing the Twin Spires in person was surreal.

And beyond the history, which the track is full of, it was just genuinely fun. Evening racing, beautiful weather, horses everywhere, and it was certainly a place where I could basically forget the rest of the world existed and stare at Thoroughbreds.

Definitely worth the 11-hour drive.

May 2026 | Kentucky Derby Museum & Churchill Downs, Louisville, Kentucky ( @derbymuseum )

Back in May, I finally visited the Kentucky Derby Museum and Churchill Downs. Being surrounded by Derby history was almost overwhelming. Trophies, silks, photographs, and artifacts connected to famous horses, jockeys, and races I had read about made everything feel more real than old footage ever could.

Standing at Churchill Downs was surreal, knowing so many horses I admire had raced there. I wanted to examine everything, especially the obscure details, and still left feeling there was more to discover. It was one of my favorite parts of the Kentucky trip, and I would gladly return.

She also took us to see the graves of several other horses buried at Walmac. At the end of the visit, she generously gave me four Walmac hats, which, of course, made me cry all over again. It was such a thoughtful gesture, and I will always treasure the kindness behind it.

Great Blue Herons are incredible hunters, often standing perfectly still before striking at fish, frogs, insects, or other small prey with lightning-fast precision. They can stand over 4 feet tall with a wingspan reaching nearly 7 feet!

Herons like Wally play an important role in local ecosystems by helping maintain balance among aquatic and wetland species. Their presence is also a good indicator of healthy habitats, as they rely on clean water and abundant food sources.

While our Thoroughbreds may be the stars of the farm, Wally is a reminder that farms are home to much more than horses. From birds and pollinators to wildlife of all kinds, these landscapes support an entire community of living things.

Today marks one year since I learned Collin ended his life. As I post this, I am in Wichita, Kansas, which is where he was when he died. He was only 31 years old and struggled deeply with depression and bipolar disorder. In the beginning of 2025, he took off on a road trip out of nowhere one day on a manic episode, ending up in various psychiatric hospitals, homeless shelters, and hotels in Kansas in the final months of his life. 

Collin always had the ability to bring out parts of people they didnât know they had in themselves. I think heâs the only person in my life I can think of that Iâve seen actively push people out of their comfort zones when it comes to things like overcoming your inner cringe, trying something youâre too scared to do, and embracing the âwhy notâ attitude? So why not come to Kansas?

I could resent and hate Kansas, but for some reason I donât enough to avoid it entirely. A lot of people might think Iâm just here âtraumamaxxing,â and to many out there, yeah, coming closer to the thing or place where your loved one k*lled themselves can be that way. But for me the trauma began when I learned the failures of our world canât be pinpointed to one place or person. Iâve been told that seeing where they died narrows it down to it being âsomewhereâ instead of âeverywhere,â but I know that it will still always feel like itâs everywhere to me. 

To me, a big part of love is learning to understand. Put your shit aside and learn to understand the other. I really had no reason to ever come to Wichita, Kansas before this, but something drove Collin to set up shop here, and I am here to understand more about that. I want to see what he saw and experience what he did while he was alive.

And sure we could just blame the illness itself, but maybe a less flashy city compared to LA eased a mind that felt like it should want more. Maybe there was comfort in being somewhere less rat racey. Maybe it was the ability to speak in a southern accent every other sentence with nobody questioning it. Maybe it was the chance to finally be someone else when you couldnât stand being yourself. If the afterlife is real, I hope we can talk about it then.

About this page, The Potential Dropout:

Day in the life of an engineering student was originally started by The Potential Dropout (me) on TikTok as a vlog series in December of 2021, in my first semester of university as a mechanical engineering student. I was failing my Calculus class at that point. Little did I know the video resonated with so many overnight, making the series a viral one on the Internet. Ever since then, hundreds of episodes came out, and the series documented my evolution as a person and a student through this challenging, yet eventful academic journey that taught me priceless lessons and shaped me into who I am today. Despite my ironic name, the series' main purpose is to help other struggling students cope and navigate through their journey and encourage them to become a better version of themselves. The main message is to not give up, no matter the setbacks. 

Iâve been documenting everything, from all-nighters and moments of failure to lessons, growth, and personal wins. Today, that journey has resonated with an audience of over 300,000 loyal followers around the world. My content has reached hundreds of millions of views. 

Since then, we've expanded to 
- Instagram (relatable STEM memes that I made or found), 
- YouTube (longer-form videos where I teach you courses and tips and tricks and offer mental health advice),
- Discord (a community of over 11k members!), 
- PATREON, where I share you my notes and other resources that helped me survive through my courses at McGill. If you want to support me, it's there! 
All links are in my bio.

Pigeons are medium-sized birds found almost everywhere humans live, especially in cities. The most common kind people see is the rock pigeon, usually gray with darker wing bands and an iridescent neck that shines green and purple in the light. Theyâre strong fliers with excellent navigation skills and were historically used to carry messages over long distances. Despite their âcity birdâ reputation, pigeons originally lived on sea cliffs and rocky areas.

Theyâre very intelligent and social birds, capable of recognizing individual humans and learning patterns. Pigeons eat mostly seeds and grains but will scavenge almost anything in urban areas. They form strong pair bonds, often mate for life, and both parents help raise their chicks by producing a nutrient-rich substance called crop milk. Basically, theyâre way smarter and more complex than people give them credit for.

With winter well upon us, letâs brighten up the season with the return of #FeatheredFriday and a throwback to some of the highlights banded at TTPBRS this year! 

First is a spectacular Golden-winged Warbler, a species at risk with a small breeding population around the Great Lakes. This young male was on his first journey down south and is hopefully hanging around a nice mangrove in Central America. 

Next, a Northern Rough-winged Swallow, an unassuming bird named for their wings being... well, rough. Itâs not visible to the eye, but the leading edge of their wings have tiny, stiff barbs that make them rough to the touch and might help with aerodynamic stability. This one was over seven years old and has probably been nesting at the park her entire life. 

Red-breasted Nuthatches arenât exactly uncommon, but what was special about them this year was the sheer number encountered â far more than usual, and all acting like they were migrating. Except nuthatches donât migrate... What we witnessed was an irruption, or a sudden change in range driven by population and food availability. 

Last is a White-eyed Vireo, a bird that is supposed to mostly be around the southern United States, not in Toronto. This one went the wrong way on migration, which is an easier mistake to make than you might guess! Luckily, when we caught it, it already had an enormous fat load, something birds only build up when they plan to fly extremely long distances, so it had probably realized its mistake and was getting ready to fly the right way. 

What was your favourite bird you spotted this year? Bonus points if you also saw it in Tommy Thompson Park.

Next, a Northern Rough-winged Swallow, an unassuming bird named for their wings being... well, rough. Itâs not visible to the eye, but the leading edge of their wings have tiny, stiff barbs that make them rough to the touch and might help with aerodynamic stability. This one was over seven years old and has probably been nesting at the park her entire life. 

Red-breasted Nuthatches arenât exactly uncommon, but what was special about them this year was the sheer number encountered â far more than usual, and all acting like they were migrating. Except nuthatches donât migrate... What we witnessed was an irruption, or a sudden change in range driven by population and food availability. 

Last is a White-eyed Vireo, a bird that is supposed to mostly be around the southern United States, not in Toronto. This one went the wrong way on migration, which is an easier mistake to make than you might guess! Luckily, when we caught it, it already had an enormous fat load, something birds only build up when they plan to fly extremely long distances, so it had probably realized its mistake and was getting ready to fly the right way. 

What was your favourite bird you spotted this year? Bonus points if you also saw it in Tommy Thompson Park.

Collin was someone who honestly struggled with being seen as âbipolar,âbut it was never about being mentally ill. It was about what it would mean to be minimized to the stigma and discrimination. And even if you do accept your diagnosis, sadly the world is still filled with people who really only understand mental health on a surface level, or just not at all.

Men especially were taught to internalize deep shame about mental illness starting with the lack of a space to talk about emotions deeply from a young age. At least that was Collinâs experience. He felt that if he accepted the label, he would be lesser than, and even if I showed him how much I loved him bipolar, depressed, or not, there was still a gap from feeling that from the rest of the world.

It is hard to live with bipolar, and Iâm not here to romanticize or glorify it just because Collin dealt with it. It can be ugly, messy, and a mindf*ck to deal with. But I also have to ask myself if I can really hate the illness fully knowing that I also had a life full of joy and memories with Collin, who had it. 

I will always love Collin, whether if he is his bucket hat manic self, self loathing inner demon, or just regular shmegular Collin. Sadly I think we still live in a world that still has no patience for people dealing with mental illness simply due to lack of education, but also because not many people share their experience loving someone dealing with it.

There is a reason why hundreds of you DM me privately sharing your stories about you, a partner, or loved one dealing with mental illness or su*cidality. And I am sure itâs because there is a fear of being misunderstood if publicized. I donât blame anyone for keeping their stories private or remaining anonymous, because yeah, it sucks to hope for a world that would understand better but still doesnât. But my partner is dead now so I have nothing left to hide. The worst already happened.
